glucose metabolism is critical in the regulation of T cell and monocyte activation and that oxidative stress is a major driver of the metabolic reprogramming of T cells and macrophages during HIV infection.
glucose metabolism is important for immune cell function and that changes in glucose metabolism contribute to immune activation, inflammation and disease progression in HIV infection.

1) HIV and other viruses can alter the metabolic pathways of their host cells; 2) HIV infection induces a state of chronic immune activation and persistent oxidative stress; 3) these conditions are associated with dysregulated metabolism of T cells and/or monocytes; 4) these conditions contribute to the development and progression of HIV disease; and 5) these conditions may be targets for therapeutic intervention.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how metabolic pathways are altered in HIV infection, and the consequences of these changes for the pathogenesis of HIV infection.
understanding how metabolic pathways are altered in immune cells during HIV infection and the role of this in HIV pathogenesis.
the metabolic status of T cells and how this may influence HIV infection and disease progression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the immune system is a metabolic organ, and that the metabolic state of immune cells is a critical determinant in immune activation, inflammation, HIV persistence, and disease progression.

the metabolic state of immune cells, particularly T cells and monocyte/macrophages, is critical to their activation status, function, and survival and is a key determinant in HIV pathogenesis and persistence.
HIV infection and its treatment with antiretrovirus drugs affect the metabolism of the immune cells, leading to chronic immune activation, inflammation and oxidative stress.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

metabolic pathways are critical for immune cell activation, differentiation and function and that dysregulation of these pathways contributes to chronic immune system activation and inflammation during HIV infection.

the metabolic state of immune cells is a critical factor in the maintenance of immune homeostasis and that the metabolic status of T cells and myeloid cells may be a key factor in HIV disease progression.

HIV infection induces a metabolic reprogramming in T cells and macrophages that is likely to contribute to persistent immune activation, inflammation, and co-morbid conditions in HIV-infected subjects.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the metabolic status of immune cells, particularly T cells and monocyte/macrophages, may play an important role in the development of immune activation and inflammation and may contribute to disease pathogenesis and progression.
metabolic changes in immune cells are a key component of HIV pathogenesis.
the interplay between metabolic and oxidative stress pathways in T cells and myeloid cells is critical for HIV pathogenesis.
